The ethnographic population which once occupied the area of the modern city of San Jose are called "Costanoan" by the anthropologists who seek to study the remnants of their culture. The term "Costanoan" is derived from the Spanish, "Costanos", meaning people of the coast. It is not the term by which the people knew themselves, but is a reference to a family of languages whose speakers occupied the area from the Golden Gate to Point Sur on the west, from Mount Diablo to the headwaters of the San Benito River on the east, along the crest of the Coast Ranges, and then turning west to include the drainage of the San Benito River, portions of the Salinas River and the lower drainages of the Carmel River (Kroeber 1925; Beeler 1970). To the north and the east the Costanoan were bordered by the Miwok. On the eastern frontier they shared their Coast Range boundary with the Yokuts. To the south, their neighbors were the Salinan groups and to the southwest, the Esselen.
The political organization of the Costanoan peoples were not such that the entire population of peoples of this language group identified in a nationalistic manner, rather, the important political organization was on a much more limited level. Kin groups, primarily the extended family, was the important political and social unit, with the tribelet as the major collective political unit of organization.
The Costanoan peoples were hunters and gatherers whose economic system was dependent upon the effective exploitation of the environment. In this, they were extremely successful, moving with the seasonal ripening of the various plant resources and with game movements. Primary village sites seem to have been located in the foothills to the west and east of present San Jose. The marsh and swampy lands of the valley were seasonally exploited for waterfowl, anadramous fishes and floral resources. Visits were made to both the bay and to the coast to secure shellfish and fish.
With the coming of the Spanish and the establishment of the missions at San Juan Bautista, Santa Clara and, later, San Franciso, the aboriginal culture was marked for extinction. The mission system was oriented for the conversion of the "savages" to the Christian religion and the Christian way of life. At first, conversion was attempted by means of persuasion. Later, force and military expeditions were employed to bring in "converts" to live in the missions. Subsequent Mexican and American administrations completed the cultural destruction initiated by the mission system.
It is upon this heritage that archaeologists seek to reconstruct the culture system of the Costanoan peoples. The remains of the villages and encampments of the Costanoan peoples and the peoples who preceded them are now the objects of study for archaeologists.
